newsitem.title: CHINA: HK's Tung in Beijing to discuss handover issues.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung in Beijing to discuss handover issues.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa arrived in Beijing on Wednesday for meetings with top Chinese officials less than two months before the British colony reverts to Chinese rule.

As Tung readied to meet Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and China's chief of Hong Kong policy Lu Ping, President Jiang Zemin issued a call to his countrymen to study the territory's mini-constitution, the Basic Law.

"Guaranteeing the stable transition of Hong Kong and its long-term prosperity and stability after the handover... will also affect peace and development in Asia and the world," the official People's Daily quoted Jiang as saying.

"If we persist in earnestly implementing the Basic Law, we can definitely create a beautiful future for Hong Kong," Jiang said. "People throughout the whole nation should earnestly study Hong Kong's Basic Law."
Hong Kong is due to revert to China on July 1 after 156 years of British colonial rule.

Tung, a shipping magnate anointed by Beijing to run post-colonial Hong Kong, was expected to discuss with Chinese officials a raft of problems he must address before the handover, ranging from controversial legal changes to immigration policies.
He is due to fly back to Hong Kong later on Wednesday.

Tung has been grappling with a major frontier security problem as a wave of illegal immigrants -- mainly children from China dodging the immigration queue to join relatives already in Hong Kong -- have swamped the territory.

China's Ministry of Public Security had issued rules to standardise procedures on mainland Chinese travelling to the wealthy territory of 6.4 million people after the handover, the Xinhua Daily Telegraph said on Wednesday.
The new immigration system would award points to applicants, who would be allowed into Hong Kong only after accumulating a certain amount, the newspaper said.
The new rules are aimed at combatting corrupt allocation of permits by greedy officials -- a major cause of the illegal child immigration wave.
"The new method...will use a computerised operating system to reduce the human element and make the application and approval work more scientific and objective," the newspaper said.
An unprecedented military-style joint immigration exercise between China and Hong Kong is planned this month on the border and at sea to try to stop infiltrators.
Tung also faces fierce debate over a clutch of draft laws he wants approved by a controversial shadow legislature set to replace Hong Kong's existing elected legislature upon the handover.

A large segment of Hong Kong's political establishment, especially pro-democracy politicians, views the Beijing-anointed provisional legislature as an illegal entity engaged in unconstitutional rivalry with the elected lawmaking body.
Tung faces stiff public opposition to the draft laws, a China-inspired plan to whittle down civil liberties by restricting protest rights and foreign funding of local political parties.

This week he reinforced his desire to curb protests when he told foreign correspondents that anti-government protests similar to massive demonstrations in Taiwan recently would not be permitted, nor would any advocating independence for Hong Kong, Taiwan or Tibet.
